Profile: Brad Binder

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We meet 24 year old South African Brad Binder, who is about to enter the world's premier motorcycle racing spectacle, the MotoGP series

Unique Selling Point:
The young South African Brad Binder is the first local rider to be offered a spot in the sought after Moto Grand Prix series in the sport's modern era. And judging from his last few years in the junior classes, experts agree that Binder has what it takes to compete against racing legends like Valentino Rossi and Marc Marquez. Before he enters the gruelling 2020 season, which will see riders compete in 20 races in 19 different countries across the globe, he'll be spending a few days in South Africa over the Christmas period, where on the 10th of December we can have two hours out of his busy schedule to interview him.

Summary:
Unlike other motorcycle racing classes where riders compete on modified factory spec machines, MotoGP bikes are thoroughbred racing motorcycles that would not be street legal or even available to purchase by the public. The MotoGP is to the motorcycle racing world what Formula 1 is to the car racing scene. Winning the MotoGP world championship literally means you're the fastest racer in the world, and the athletes competing here earn huge money to risk life and limb for the sport's ultimate honour. It's a truly unique achievement to be one of the chosen few to compete in the championship, because only the best of the best ever get anywhere near. For Binder it will not only be the biggest challenge of his racing career, he'll need to adapt fast to the whirlwind world of MotoGP - with millions of fans worldwide, massive television and sponsorship deals and the top manufacturer's expecting only the best from their riders. Will he stand up to the pressure?

Further information:
We have been given permission to shoot the interview with Brad Binder at the Redstar Raceway on the 10th of December, where he will be hosting a trackday sponsored by KTM (the same team he'll be racing for in 2020 MotoGP)
We'll get to see him in action on a street bike, interacting with other riders, giving tips etc.
The track will make a great setting for the interview.
We've approached Supersport re footage of Binder in action.

Press Release:


On the Grid – Brad Binder
As a teenager he took on and beat some of the fastest racers in the country. Now South African Motorcycle Racer Brad Binder is a man on a mission as he prepares for the biggest challenge of his career - facing off against legends of the sport like Valentino Rossi and Marc Márquez in this year's prestigious international MotoGP championship - becoming the first South African entrant in nearly four decades.
Producer: Graham Coetzer | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


Brad Binder Profile
06 Jan 2020
1st Draft Script

Sound Up Racing
OUT Words: Brad Binder who gets his first win in the class!

Voice
Its fast, loud and dangerous - Grand Prix Motorcycle racing is the absolute pinnacle of two wheeled competition sport - and the top-tier MotoGP class attracts a worldwide television viewership of 400 million people every year. This year’s season will see 22 riders compete in 20 races across the globe, all in the hope of being crowned the next world champion. And amongst the chosen few, 24 year old South African Brad Binder will be lining up on the grid right along side the best in the world, having just graduated to MotoGP after a successful 2019 season in the junior Moto2 class. We met Binder shortly after his return from Valencia in Spain, where he’d just had his first test on a MotoGP machine.

Sound Up Brad
Brad: You know I pulled out the pits and there I am, I had Valentino Rossi on one side, Marc Marquez was there…

Mac: Marc Marquez, geez.

Brad: You know these guys are people I’ve looked up to my whole life, they’re the legends of the sport. And then you… I find myself on track with them, so I was just like gosh, you know, we’ve come a long way.

Link
MotoGP is a serious game, here he’s going to race against the likes of Valentino Rossi as well as Marc Marquez and this, is the big league.

Voice
If riders do well in the slower Moto3 and Moto2 classes of the sport, a lucky few manage to be signed by one of the premier MotoGP teams. These bikes generate 280 horsepower and have been clocked doing in excess of 350km/h. To put that into perspective, at those speeds if you close your eyes for a second you will have travelled nearly a 100m without seeing a thing.

Sound Up Brad
They’re the “Formula 1 cars of bikes” you know, it’s the top of the top. The first time you open that throttle it’s almost shock I promise you. It’s another world.

Voice
It certainly is a far cry from the quiet streets of Potchefstroom where he was born. Binder says the need for speed has been with him ever since he can remember.

Sound Up Brad
I actually originally started racing properly in go-karts, I did karting when I was 6 or 7 years old. And as soon as I was old enough to start racing road bikes, I swopped over. And I just preferred two wheels, and that’s about it.

Voice
And by all accounts he was fast even way back then. Robert Portman is the editor of Ride Fast Magazine, has won several South African categories of motorcycle racing and has known Binder since he was still a rookie racer.

Sound Up Robert Portman
I met Brad, like I said, when he was 9 years old, and him and his brother Darren was seven at the time

Voice
Darryn Binder, Brad’s younger brother, is currently also competing in the Moto3 championship. Portman, who played mentor to the brothers in their early careers, says Brad was unbelievably fast even as a young teenager still in braces.

Sound Up Robert
Robert: He was 14 years old, first time in a national, he was about this big, and I was this top hotshot National SuperSport racer, I was the man to beat on my Triumph. And this 14 year old came, on his Suzuki machine, with his dad prepping it. Come race day, at the start, I’m out front thinking I’ve got this, and a 14 year old “braceface” comes past me, smiling, shining those braces in my face, and passing me for the lead of a National Superbike 600 Supersport race…

Mac: At 14 years old?

Robert: At the age of 14 years old.

Mac: Wow

Robert: That’s when we kind of knew well this guy is just going on to bigger and better things.

Voice
Motor racing is extremely expensive, especially for South Africans trying to make a name for themselves overseas. Binder says his dad Trevor and mom Sharon played a huge role in getting him to where he is today.

Sound Up Brad
Without my family, I would have been nowhere. My dad and my mom are absolutely incredible. You know the amount of sacrifices they made for me to get to where I am today, especially at the beginning, was absolutely insane. You know my mom was living with me in Europe, my little brother was tiny at the time.

Voice
By 2009, Binder was competing in the Red Bull Moto GP Rookies Cup, an international competition that is a feeder series for the worldwide MotoGP series. But competing against some of the best riders in the world, most of them with very deep pockets, was never going to be easy.

Sound Up Brad
It was hard. At the beginning, to find our feet in Europe was difficult. When I got their I wasn’t great at all. I was really quick in South Africa, and when we went that side we expected to get the same results as we got here kind of thing, but it wasn’t the case, you know you’ve got to start somewhere.


Voice
But hard work, determination and a reputation for being fast and fearless got him noticed in the MotoGP arena, where he started off in the junior Moto3 class in 2012. 2016 was a massive turning point in his career, when he was crowned the Moto3 world champion, graduating to the faster Moto2 series for 2017. Last year he finished second in the Moto2 world championship, winning the last few races of the year. And just a few weeks later came the big announcement - Brad would be the first South African since 1983 to compete in the prestigious MotoGP class, having signed with the Redbull KTM Factory Racing Team.

Link Mac
Racing in MotoGP is no small feat, but listen to this stat. There have been more people in space, then there have been actual riders that have made it onto MotoGp in this modern era, wow.

Voice
Donovan Fourie is the host of DSTV’s The Bike Show, and a fanatic fan of all things MotoGP.

Sound Up Donovan
Mac: It’s actually almost like a moving circus, because they go from country to country, and race?

Donovan: Ja it is just a village that moves absolutely everywhere, and I mean the costs involved are spectacular. I was looking up, researching one of the teams. The Repsol Honda Team, which is sort of Marquez, the championship winning team, and their budget for they year, I mean it’s estimated of course because they don’t really release it, it was something like R1.2 billion.

Voice
The spectacle that is MotoGP is filled with glitz and glamour, but with major brands spending this kind of money, the drivers lives are anything but easy. Binder’s biggest challenge for the upcoming season might be more off the track than on it.

Sound Up Brad
I leave my house on a wednesday, I arrive at the track hopefully, depending on how far it is, on a wednesday night. Our schedule on a thursday is insane, things are like within 45 minute time slots of different interviews, signings. And then from then on, you know on Friday all the riding starts, and then sunday night when you done the race you literally, you get out of the suit as quick as you can, you get into the car back to the airport, back to our base in Spain so you can start training again on the monday.

Voice
In the late 70’s legendary South African rider Kork Ballington, who was recently inducted into the MotoGP hall of fame, managed to win the 1978 and 79 MotoGP world titles. Today’s bikes are so fast and powerful, they put huge demands on riders bodies, and racers can lose up to 4kg in bodyweight during a single race. If Binder hopes to follow in Ballington’s footsteps, he’ll have to achieve a level of fitness many of us can only dream of.

Sound Up Brad
I’ve just come back from a training camp in Austria, where they do every test under the sun, I mean we’ve got nutritionists now, we’ve got physical trainers

Voice
According to Portman, who accompanied Brad to his first MotoGP testing session last year, the talk in the paddock is that Binder is hot property at the moment.

Sound Up Robert
Brad was on not the best bike in Moto3 at one stage, not in the best team, but he made it work and that’s what put him in the shop window. These teams don’t just look at what’s happening on track, it’s also off track, the maturity he shows to do all the PR stuff, and that is what makes him such a big attraction and that’s whats going to make him one of the top boys in MotoGP.

Voice
Brad, who still takes time out of his hectic schedule to come and coach young South African riders back home, says he will spend his first year amongst the big boys getting to know the ropes. But perhaps most importantly, he believes he has what it takes to bring home the World Championship title.

Sound Up Brad
You have to be in it to win it, these are the best guys in the world, I would never have got there if I wasn’t decent. So let’s see. I hope I can give them something and make sure that we see the South African flag on top of the podium. Hopefully sometime soon.

And then from then on, you know on Friday all the riding starts, and then sunday night when you done the race you literally, you get out of the suit as quick as you can, you get into the car back to the airport, back to our base in Spain so you can start training again on the monday. Voice In the late 70’s legendary South African rider Kork Ballington, who was recently inducted into the MotoGP hall of fame, managed to win the 1978 and 79 MotoGP world titles. Today’s bikes are so fast and powerful, they put huge demands on riders bodies, and racers can lose up to 4kg in bodyweight during a single race. If Binder hopes to follow in Ballington’s footsteps, he’ll have to achieve a level of fitness many of us can only dream of. Sound Up Brad I’ve just come back from a training camp in Austria, where they do every test under the sun, I mean we’ve got nutritionists now, we’ve got physical trainers Voice According to Portman, who accompanied Brad to his first MotoGP testing session last year, the talk in the paddock is that Binder is hot property at the moment. Sound Up Robert Brad was on not the best bike in Moto3 at one stage, not in the best team, but he made it work and that’s what put him in the shop window. These teams don’t just look at what’s happening on track, it’s also off track, the maturity he shows to do all the PR stuff, and that is what makes him such a big attraction and that’s whats going to make him one of the top boys in MotoGP. Voice Brad, who still takes time out of his hectic schedule to come and coach young South African riders back home, says he will spend his first year amongst the big boys getting to know the ropes. But perhaps most importantly, he believes he has what it takes to bring home the World Championship title. Sound Up Brad You have to be in it to win it, these are the best guys in the world, I would never have got there if I wasn’t decent. So let’s see. I hope I can give them something and make sure that we see the South African flag on top of the podium. Hopefully sometime soon.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We meet 24 year old South African Brad Binder, who is about to enter the world's premier motorcycle racing spectacle, the MotoGP series
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The young South African Brad Binder is the first local rider to be offered a spot in the sought after Moto Grand Prix series in the sport's modern era. And judging from his last few years in the junior classes, experts agree that Binder has what it takes to compete against racing legends like Valentino Rossi and Marc Marquez. Before he enters the gruelling 2020 season, which will see riders compete in 20 races in 19 different countries across the globe, he'll be spending a few days in South Africa over the Christmas period, where on the 10th of December we can have two hours out of his busy schedule to interview him.
metadata.Summary: Unlike other motorcycle racing classes where riders compete on modified factory spec machines, MotoGP bikes are thoroughbred racing motorcycles that would not be street legal or even available to purchase by the public. The MotoGP is to the motorcycle racing world what Formula 1 is to the car racing scene. Winning the MotoGP world championship literally means you're the fastest racer in the world, and the athletes competing here earn huge money to risk life and limb for the sport's ultimate honour. It's a truly unique achievement to be one of the chosen few to compete in the championship, because only the best of the best ever get anywhere near. For Binder it will not only be the biggest challenge of his racing career, he'll need to adapt fast to the whirlwind world of MotoGP - with millions of fans worldwide, massive television and sponsorship deals and the top manufacturer's expecting only the best from their riders. Will he stand up to the pressure?
metadata.Further information: We have been given permission to shoot the interview with Brad Binder at the Redstar Raceway on the 10th of December, where he will be hosting a trackday sponsored by KTM (the same team he'll be racing for in 2020 MotoGP) We'll get to see him in action on a street bike, interacting with other riders, giving tips etc. The track will make a great setting for the interview. We've approached Supersport re footage of Binder in action.
